title: Mathematical Methods
body:
MATH 3200 rebuilds calculus for functions of several variables. [[CALCULUS 1]] and
[[CALCULUS 2]] both worked with $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$, one number in and one number
out, and almost nothing real has that shape. Temperature varies with position in three
directions and with time. A cost depends on every parameter of a model at once.

Three things change. A slope becomes a [[Gradient]], since a surface has a different slope in
every direction. An integral becomes an integral over a region, along a path, or through a
surface. An equation relating a function to its derivatives becomes a
[[Partial Differential Equations|PDE]] describing a field varying in space and time.

The course has five blocks: [[Vector Calculus]],
[[Multivariable Optimization|optimisation in several variables]],
[[Differential Equations|systems of ODEs]], a rigorous revisit of convergence, and an
introduction to PDEs. Vector calculus is the largest and the one the others lean on.

For a CS degree this is where the mathematics behind machine learning lives.
[[Gradient Descent]] is [[Multivariable Optimization]] with no closed form available,
[[Back Propagation]] is the [[Multivariable Chain Rule]] applied layer by layer, and
[[Principal Component Analysis]] is a [[Lagrange Multipliers]] problem whose multiplier turns
out to be an eigenvalue.

## Topics

### Differentiating a surface

A [[Partial Derivative]] is the ordinary derivative taken with the other variables held
constant, so it introduces no new technique and a great deal of new bookkeeping:

$$
f(x,y) = x^2 + y^2 \qquad
\frac{\partial f}{\partial x} = 2x \qquad
\frac{\partial f}{\partial y} = 2y
$$

Clairaut's theorem gives $f_{xy} = f_{yx}$ when the mixed partials are continuous, so the
order of differentiation does not matter and the bookkeeping stays manageable.

The [[Gradient]] collects the partials into a vector:

$$
\nabla f = \left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}, \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}\right)
= (2x, 2y), \qquad \nabla f(1,2) = (2,4)
$$

That vector points along steepest ascent, its magnitude $\sqrt{20} \approx 4.47$ is how steep
that ascent is, and it is perpendicular to the level curve through the point. The rate of
change in any chosen direction is the directional derivative
$D_{\mathbf{u}}f = \nabla f\cdot\mathbf{u}$ for a unit vector $\mathbf{u}$, which is largest
when $\mathbf{u}$ points along the gradient, since a dot product is maximised by alignment.
That single fact is what every gradient-based optimiser exploits.

The [[Multivariable Chain Rule]] contributes one term per path through the dependency tree,
with each term a product along that path. If $z$ depends on $x$ and $y$, and both depend on
$t$:

$$
\frac{dz}{dt} = \frac{\partial z}{\partial x}\frac{dx}{dt} + \frac{\partial z}{\partial y}\frac{dy}{dt}
$$

[[Back Propagation]] is an efficient implementation of that rule on a tree with millions of
paths. [[Differential]] covers the elements $dx$, $ds$, $d\mathbf{r}$, $dA$, $dV$ and $dS$,
and choosing the right one is usually the harder half of setting up an integral.

### Finding maxima and minima

[[Multivariable Optimization]] locates critical points where $\nabla f = \mathbf{0}$, meaning
the surface is level in every direction at once, and then classifies them. With
$D = f_{xx}f_{yy} - f_{xy}^2$ evaluated at the point:

```
D > 0 and f_xx > 0   minimum
D > 0 and f_xx < 0   maximum
D < 0                saddle, up in one direction and down in another
D = 0                the test decides nothing
```

The saddle has no one-variable analogue, and $f(x,y) = x^2 - y^2$ at the origin is the
standard case: a curve along the $x$-axis sees a minimum and a curve along the $y$-axis sees a
maximum. It is also why an optimiser can stall somewhere that is not a minimum at all.

[[Lagrange Multipliers]] handles optimisation subject to a constraint, and it follows from one
geometric fact. At a constrained optimum the level curve of $f$ is tangent to the constraint
curve, so their gradients point the same way:

$$
\nabla f = \lambda \nabla g \quad\text{subject to}\quad g = k
$$

Maximising $xy$ subject to $x + y = 10$:

```
∇f = (y, x),  ∇g = (1, 1)      so  y = λ  and  x = λ,  giving x = y
constraint:  x + y = 10        so  x = y = 5
maximum:     xy = 25
```

Every other pair summing to 10 gives a smaller product, which the constraint alone would have
required checking one at a time. The multiplier is itself a rate of change, equal to
$df^*/dk$, so it says how much the optimum improves as the constraint loosens, which gives it a meaning
in the problem being solved.

### Vector calculus

[[Vector Calculus]] contains three operators, three kinds of integral, and three theorems
relating them. A [[Vector Field]] assigns a vector to every point, which is what
[[LINEAR ALGEBRA]]'s vectors become when they vary from place to place, such as wind velocity
across a map.

The three operators are distinguished by what goes in and what comes out:

| Operator | Input | Output | Measures |
|---|---|---|---|
| $\nabla f$ | scalar field | vector field | direction of steepest increase |
| $\nabla\cdot\mathbf{F}$, [[Divergence]] | vector field | scalar field | flux per unit volume, so a source or a sink |
| $\nabla\times\mathbf{F}$, [[Curl]] | vector field | vector field | circulation per unit area, so local rotation |

Checking the shape catches most errors before any arithmetic starts. Two identities follow
from equality of mixed partials: $\nabla\times(\nabla f) = \mathbf{0}$, so a gradient field
never rotates, and $\nabla\cdot(\nabla\times\mathbf{F}) = 0$.

A [[Conservative Vector Field]] is one that is a gradient. Being a gradient, having path
independent line integrals, and having every closed-loop integral vanish are all equivalent,
which is why work done against gravity depends only on height gained. A vanishing curl joins
that list only on a simply connected domain, with
$\langle -y, x\rangle/(x^2+y^2)$ as the counterexample on a domain with a hole.

[[Parameterization]] describes a curve by one parameter and a surface by two, and every
integral below is evaluated by parameterising first. A [[Line Integral]] runs along a path,
where $\int_C f\,ds$ is [[Arc Length]] carrying a weight and
$\int_C\mathbf{F}\cdot d\mathbf{r}$ measures work. The vector version flips sign when the
direction of travel reverses and the scalar version does not. A [[Surface Integral]] raises
both kinds by one dimension, where orientation becomes a choice of which side is outward.
[[Flux]] is what the vector surface integral measures and is the quantity divergence is the
density of.

[[Multiple Integration]] covers double and triple integrals, evaluated one variable at a time:

$$
\int_0^1\!\!\int_0^2 xy \,dy\,dx
= \int_0^1 x\left[\tfrac{y^2}{2}\right]_0^2 dx
= \int_0^1 2x\,dx = 1
$$

Limits are read from the inside out, where the innermost may depend on both outer variables
and the outermost has to be constant. Fubini's theorem permits reordering, and one of the six
orders of a triple integral is usually far easier than the others. Volume elements are
$r\,dr\,d\theta\,dz$ in cylindrical coordinates and
$\rho^2\sin\phi\,d\rho\,d\phi\,d\theta$ in spherical, where the extra factor is the Jacobian, a
[[Determinant]], present because changing coordinates stretches volume by exactly that amount.

### One theorem, stated four ways

The organising result of the course is that the integral of a derivative over a region equals
the original object evaluated on that region's boundary:

| Theorem | Region | Boundary |
|---|---|---|
| [[Fundamental Theorem of Calculus\|FTC]] | an interval | its two endpoints |
| [[Green's Theorem]] | a region in the plane | the curve around it |
| [[Stokes' Theorem]] | a surface in space | the curve around its rim |
| [[Divergence Theorem]] | a solid | the surface enclosing it |

Learning them as four theorems costs four times what learning them as one costs.

[[Green's Theorem]] gives $\oint_C P\,dx + Q\,dy = \iint_D (Q_x - P_y)\,dA$ with $C$ traversed
counterclockwise, and setting $P=0$ and $Q=x$ computes the area of any region from a walk
around its edge, which is how a planimeter works. [[Stokes' Theorem]] gives
$\oint_{\partial S}\mathbf{F}\cdot d\mathbf{r} = \iint_S(\nabla\times\mathbf{F})\cdot d\mathbf{S}$,
where the right side depends only on the boundary, so any convenient surface with that
boundary can be substituted. The [[Divergence Theorem]] gives
$\iint_{\partial E}\mathbf{F}\cdot d\mathbf{S} = \iiint_E(\nabla\cdot\mathbf{F})\,dV$ for a
closed surface, and it is what derives the [[Heat Equation]] from the physical statement that
heat leaving a region is heat the region lost.

### Ordinary differential equations

[[Differential Equations]] indexes the block and holds the classification, by order, linearity,
homogeneity and whether the coefficients are constant, along with the table mapping each class
to a method.

[[Homogeneous ODE]] covers constant coefficients, where the roots of $ar^2+br+c=0$ decide
everything:

$$
y'' - 3y' + 2y = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; r^2 - 3r + 2 = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; r = 1, 2
\;\Rightarrow\; y = c_1e^{t} + c_2e^{2t}
$$

Distinct real roots give that form, a repeated root gives $c_1e^{rt}+c_2te^{rt}$, and complex
roots $\alpha\pm\beta i$ give $e^{\alpha t}(c_1\cos\beta t + c_2\sin\beta t)$, which is what
oscillation looks like algebraically: the imaginary part becomes the frequency and the real
part becomes the decay.

[[Non-Homogeneous ODE]] adds a particular solution to the complementary one, giving
$y = y_c + y_p$, which is the same structure theorem as one particular solution plus the null
space for $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$. Initial conditions are applied to the sum.
[[Undetermined Coefficients]] guesses the shape of the forcing term, using the full polynomial
and both sine and cosine, and multiplies by $t$ when a guessed term already appears in $y_c$,
which is the algebraic signature of resonance. [[Cauchy-Euler]] handles the
variable-coefficient family that still solves in closed form.

[[Systems of Differential Equations]] is where [[LINEAR ALGEBRA]] pays off. Coupled equations
$\mathbf{x}' = A\mathbf{x}$ decouple in the eigenvector basis: each eigenpair contributes
$e^{\lambda t}\mathbf{v}$, and the general solution is their linear combination.
[[Diagonalization]] turns $n$ interacting equations into $n$ independent ones.
[[Phase Portrait]] then reads stability off the eigenvalues with no solving at all, since every
eigenvalue having a negative real part means every mode decays, complex eigenvalues spiral,
and real eigenvalues of opposite sign give a saddle. [[Series Solutions]] handles the rest with
a power series when nothing else applies.

### Convergence, revisited

This block adds no notes deliberately. The sequence and series machinery belongs to
[[CALCULUS 2]] and is used here: [[Sequence]], [[Infinite Series]], [[Convergence Tests]],
[[Power Series]] and [[Taylor Series]]. What this course adds is the consequence. A
[[Series Solutions|series solution]] carries no information outside its radius of convergence,
and a mode expansion of a PDE is an infinite sum whose convergence decides whether the model
says anything at the boundary.

### Partial differential equations

A PDE has several independent variables, so its general solution carries arbitrary functions
where an ODE carries arbitrary constants, and pinning it down needs conditions along a whole
boundary.

Separation of variables is the method taught. Assume the solution factors as
$u(x,t) = X(x)T(t)$, substitute, and divide, which leaves a function of $x$ equal to a function
of $t$. Two functions of different variables can only be equal by both being constant, and that
constant splits the PDE into two ODEs the previous block already solved. The boundary
conditions then select which modes are allowed, and a [[Fourier Series]] fits the initial data
to them.

Three equations carry the block:

```
u_t = k u_xx      Heat Equation:     diffuses and smooths, cannot be run backwards
u_tt = c² u_xx    Wave Equation:     propagates at speed c, loses nothing
∇²u = 0           Laplace's Equation: the steady state of the first
```

One extra time derivative is the whole difference between the first two, and it changes
everything about their behaviour. The [[Heat Equation]] destroys information, so two different
starting temperatures can converge to the same distribution and the past cannot be recovered.
The [[Wave Equation]] preserves shapes travelling in both directions. [[Laplace's Equation]]
has harmonic solutions that equal their own average over any circle, which forces their extreme
values onto the boundary, since an interior maximum would exceed its own neighbourhood
average.

## Related courses

- [[CALCULUS 1]] (MATH 1200) and [[CALCULUS 2]] (MATH 2200) are the prerequisites. Calc 2
  introduces [[Partial Derivative]], [[Gradient]], the [[Multivariable Chain Rule]] and first
  and second order [[Differential Equations]] and passes all of them here, while keeping the
  [[Double Integral]] and the convergence material. Every technique in
  [[Integration Techniques]] is a working prerequisite, since solving anything here ends in an
  integral.
- [[LINEAR ALGEBRA]] (MATH 1203) supplies more than it appears to. [[Vector]] and
  [[Dot Product]] are the algebra every operator is written in, the [[Determinant]] is the
  curl cross product and the Jacobian and the Hessian test, [[Vector Space]] and
  [[Linear Dependence]] are why a general solution is a linear combination, and
  [[Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors]] with [[Diagonalization]] are the method for
  [[Systems of Differential Equations]].
- [[LINEAR ALGEBRA FOR DATA SCIENCE]] (MATH 2303) reaches the second-derivative test from the
  other direction, since definiteness of a [[Quadratic Form]] is the Hessian criterion stated
  in eigenvalues, which is the version that survives past two variables.
- [[FOURIER AND COMPLEX ANALYSIS]] (MATH 4199) continues where separation of variables stops.
  The modes it produces are [[Orthogonal Functions]], and writing an initial condition in that
  basis is a [[Fourier Series]] with [[Fourier Coefficients]] given by integrals.
  [[Line Integral]] and [[Parameterization]] are the real-variable rehearsal for contour
  integration there.
- [[MACHINE LEARNING]] and the neural network notes in [[THE NEW TURING OMNIBUS]] run on this
  course, where [[Gradient Descent]] is [[Multivariable Optimization]] without a closed form,
  [[Back Propagation]] is the chain rule on a large dependency tree, [[Loss Function]] is the
  $f$ being minimised, and saddle points are a practical obstacle.
- [[STATISTICS]] (MATH 2234) normalises a joint [[Probability Density Function]] with a double
  integral and computes marginals by integrating out a variable, so [[Multiple Integration]] is
  what makes multivariate probability computable.
- [[COMPUTING MACHINERY]] (COMP 2655) and [[ALGORITHMS AND COMPLEXITY]] solve these equations
  numerically, where a discretised [[Laplace's Equation]] is a large sparse
  [[System of Linear Equations]] and the error is bounded by a truncated [[Taylor Series]].
- [[CLASSICAL PHYSICS 1]] (PHYS 1201) is where a [[Conservative Vector Field]] is first met
  without the name. Gravity is one, [[Potential Energy]] is the scalar field it comes from,
  and [[Friction]] is the non-conservative case that breaks
  [[Conservation of Energy]].
